title: The Potter's Secret Glaze
summary: A girl apprenticing with her aunt, a skilled potter, experiments for weeks to recreate a beautiful blue glaze from an old family heirloom pot, learning about clay, heat, and minerals along the way.
poll: Trying something over and over after it fails is a waste of time.

versions.title: The Potter's Secret Glaze
versions.text:
Noor is a girl. She helps her aunt Hind. Aunt Hind is a potter.

A potter makes pots from clay. Aunt Hind has a small shop.

One day, Noor sees an old pot. It is a family pot. It has a bright blue glaze. Noor loves its color.

"How did you make this blue?" Noor asks.

"I do not know," says Aunt Hind. "That old glaze is a secret now."

Noor wants to find the secret. She starts to help Aunt Hind each day. She learns to shape wet clay. She learns about heat in the big kiln.

Noor tries a blue glaze. It comes out gray. She tries again. It cracks in the heat.

Noor does not give up. She keeps trying new mixes. She changes the heat each time.

At last, one pot comes out of the kiln. It is a deep, bright blue! It looks just like the old family pot.

Aunt Hind smiles at Noor. "You found it," she says. Noor feels so proud.

versions.title: The Potter's Secret Glaze
versions.text:
Noor spends every summer as an apprentice in her aunt's small pottery workshop. She loves the smell of wet clay and the warmth of the kiln.

A potter shapes clay into pots, bowls, and jars, then fires each piece in a hot kiln. Aunt Hind has run this dusty little shop for many years.

One quiet afternoon, Noor notices an old family pot on a high shelf. It has a bright blue glaze unlike anything she has seen before. She cannot stop staring at its deep, shining color.

"How did you make this glaze?" Noor asks.

"Honestly, I do not know," Aunt Hind admits, sighing. "That recipe is a secret now, lost long before I was born."

Determined, Noor decides to find the secret glaze herself. She begins helping her aunt every day after school. She learns to shape wet clay and to understand how different minerals change a glaze's color.

Still, Noor refuses to give up. Week after week, she adjusts her mixture, changing one mineral or the heat just a little each time.

Finally, one pot comes out of the kiln glowing with a deep, bright blue, just like the old family pot.

Aunt Hind beams with pride. "You finally solved it," she says, hugging her patient young apprentice.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Noor decides that pottery is too hard and gives up on her aunt's craft after her first day.

Aunt Hind refuses to let Noor near the kiln, so the girl never learns how pots are fired.
The old family pot is accidentally broken during the story, and Noor spends the days crying.

wrong.A: Noor keeps working hard instead of giving up.
wrong.C: Aunt Hind welcomes Noor's help in the workshop.
wrong.D: The old pot stays safe on the shelf the whole story.

questions.stem: What does Noor do every day to learn the potter's craft?

She helps her aunt and learns to shape clay
She travels to other towns for lessons

questions.stem: Why does Noor's second attempt at the glaze crack in the kiln?

The intense heat damages the fragile pot

wrong.C: No accident with Aunt Hind is mentioned.
wrong.D: Pots are glazed, not painted, in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, the word experiment most nearly means —

a tool used in the kiln to lift pots

questions.stem: Why does Noor keep changing just one mineral or the temperature at a time?

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of this story?

wrong.B: The story does not list facts about different clays.
wrong.D: The story covers one summer, not a full year.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why Aunt Hind feels proud at the end of the story?
options: Noor used a completely different craft than pottery
Noor's patient, careful experiments finally succeeded
Noor bought a new glaze from the market
Noor was lucky and never actually tried hard
questions.why: Aunt Hind's pride comes from watching Noor's determined, patient work finally pay off.

wrong.A: Noor stays within the pottery craft the whole story.
wrong.C: Noor makes the glaze herself rather than buying it.
wrong.D: Noor's success comes from weeks of hard, careful work.

MID.prompt: Explain how Noor's patient habits as an apprentice helped her finally recreate the secret glaze. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Noor's habits led to her success.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Noor's patient habits as an apprentice are the reason she finally recreated the secret glaze. Every day, she helped her aunt and learned how different minerals and the kiln's temperature changed a glaze's color. When her first experiment came out gray and her second pot cracked, she did not quit; instead, she adjusted just one small thing at a time so she could understand what was working. Because she kept careful track of her changes over many weeks, she was eventually able to match the old family pot's deep blue glaze.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A ceramic apprentice abandons a long family tradition out of frustration.
A workshop owner refuses to teach her craft to any apprentice.
A family pot is sold at the market for a large sum of money.
A patient apprentice recreates a lost glaze through persistent trial and error.
questions.why: The story traces Noor's persistent, methodical experimentation until she successfully recreates the lost glaze.

wrong.B: Aunt Hind actively teaches Noor throughout the story.

questions.stem: According to the story, why is the original glaze recipe no longer known?
options: Aunt Hind refuses to share it with anyone
It was lost generations before Aunt Hind was born
It was written in a language no one can read
A rival potter stole and destroyed the recipe
questions.why: Aunt Hind explains that the recipe was lost before she was even born, passed down imperfectly.

wrong.A: Aunt Hind genuinely does not know the recipe herself.
wrong.C: No mention is made of any written language issue.
wrong.D: No rival potter appears anywhere in the story.

questions.stem: What was the specific cause of Noor's second failed pot?
options: She forgot to add any minerals to the mixture of clay and water
An overly intense kiln temperature cracked the piece
She used clay that had already hardened in the bowl
Her aunt accidentally dropped the pot on the floor

wrong.C: The clay itself is not described as already hardened.
wrong.D: No accident involving Aunt Hind occurs.

questions.stem: In the story, the phrase trial and error most closely describes a process of —
options: copying an exact method from a trusted book of rules
repeatedly testing and adjusting until something works
giving up after the very first attempt fails badly
asking an expert to solve the problem for them
questions.why: Noor's repeated experiments, each adjusted slightly, exemplify learning through trial and error.

wrong.A: No book provides the method in this story.
wrong.C: Noor continues well past her first failure.
wrong.D: Noor solves the problem herself, not through an expert.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why does Noor change only one variable at a time in her mixture?
options: So that she can clearly identify which change affects the outcome
Because her aunt insists on this exact method for every test and rule
Because she lacks enough minerals to change more than one thing at once
So that she can finish her experiments more quickly and go home early
questions.why: Isolating one variable at a time is how Noor can tell which adjustment actually changes the glaze's color.

wrong.B: The story credits this method to Noor's own approach.
wrong.C: A shortage of minerals is never mentioned.
wrong.D: Her method actually extends the process over many weeks.

questions.stem: In what order did these events occur in the story?
options: Noor finds success, she tries her first glaze, the pot cracks
Noor notices the old pot, her first glaze turns gray, she finally succeeds
Aunt Hind reveals the recipe, Noor copies it exactly, the glaze works
The pot cracks, Noor becomes an apprentice, she notices the old pot
questions.why: Noor first notices the old pot, then fails with a gray glaze, and eventually succeeds after many trials.

wrong.A: Success comes last in the story, not first.
wrong.C: Aunt Hind never reveals a working recipe to copy.
wrong.D: Noor is already an apprentice before noticing the pot.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about Aunt Hind's workshop from how she responds to Noor's curiosity?
options: The workshop discourages apprentices from asking questions
The workshop supports an apprentice's independent exploration
The workshop forbids any failed experiments
The workshop relies only on exact written instructions
questions.why: Aunt Hind allows Noor to experiment freely in the workshop, supporting her curiosity rather than limiting it.

wrong.A: Aunt Hind answers Noor's question honestly and openly.
wrong.C: Noor's failed attempts are an accepted part of her learning.
wrong.D: No written instructions exist for the lost recipe.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with Aunt Hind embracing Noor after her success?
options: To suggest the ceramic tradition will now be abandoned by the whole family
To imply that the glaze's color does not actually matter to anyone in the town
To emphasize that Noor's determined effort restored something meaningful
To show that Aunt Hind had secretly known the recipe all along
questions.why: The warm ending highlights how Noor's persistence successfully revived a treasured family tradition.

wrong.A: The tradition is revived, not abandoned, by the ending.
wrong.B: The specific blue color matters greatly throughout the story.
wrong.D: Aunt Hind genuinely did not know the recipe beforehand.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says trying something over and over after it fails is a waste of time. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Noor's experiments.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that trying something over and over after it fails is a waste of time. In the story, Noor's first glaze came out gray and her second pot cracked in the kiln, yet neither failure was wasted, because each one taught her something about how minerals and temperature affected the final color. By patiently changing one part of her mixture at a time, she used her earlier failures to guide her later attempts, which is exactly how she eventually recreated the family's lost blue glaze. Someone might argue that repeated failure just wastes clay and time, but without Noor's persistent trial and error, the family tradition tied to that glaze would have stayed lost forever.
